newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Karachi bourse urges investment by institutions.
newsitem.headline: Karachi bourse urges investment by institutions.

text.p: The Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) urged financial institutions on Wednesday to invest in Pakistani stocks to pull the market out of its current lows.

"The stock prices are at low levels, but the problem is who will take the lead," asked KSE president Arif Habib at a presentation. "If financial institutions take the lead, foreigners will follow," he added.

The KSE-100 share index that is hovering around 1,500 point level at present has shed over 260 points from this year high of 1,775.57 on February 20. On Wednesday, the index edged down 0.58 points, or 0.04 to a provisional close of 1,512.47 points.
Dealers said sentiment was weak and trading volume had shrunk on lack of support from the institutions and the investors before the 1997/98 (July-June) budget due in June.
Habib said the weakness of local institutions was a major problem that dragged down stock prices during recent months.
"On an average, local institutions invest 7.0 to 8.0 billion rupees every year in stocks... but this year they have disinvested about 6.0 billion rupees."
The state-owned National Investment Trust (NIT) alone had disinvested about 3.0 billion rupees, he said.
"There is a lot of concern both here and abroad about this situation," Habib said. "Despite government measures to boost the stock market, there has been no impact," he added.
He said the market was reflecting the economic conditions of the country, which was passing through its worst period.
Habib said declining corporate profits in major sectors like textile were another problem faced by the market.
"As a result of the government packages we are likely to see an improvement in textile sector and more stress should be made on the improvement of corporate profits."
He said it was not difficult to improve a small market like KSE with capiatlisation of around $12 billion out of which almost 50 percent was held by the government or the management.
"What we need is aggressive marketing now," Habib said.
